The imag- ing and display system 1 further includes a 2D synthesizer that operates substantially in parallel with the reconstruction engine for generating 2D images that simulate mam- mograms taken at any orientation (e.g., CC or MLO) using a combination of one or more Tp and/or Tr images. The synthesized 2D images may be generated dynamically prior to display (as shown in FIG. 1) or may be stored in storage system 2 for later use. The synthesized 2D images are interchangeably referenced as T2d and Ms. The reconstruc- tion engine 3 and 2D synthesizer are preferably connected to a display system 5 via a fast transmission link. The originally acquired Mp and/or Tp images may also be forwarded to the display system 5 for concurrent or toggled viewing with the respective Tr and/or Ms images by a medical professional. [0036] Mode filters 7a, 7b are disposed between image acquisition and image display. Each of the filters 7a and 7b may additionally include customized filters for each type of image (i.e., Tp, Mp, Tr) arranged to identify and highlight certain aspects of the respective image types. In this manner, each imaging mode can be tuned or configured in an optimal way for a specific purpose. Addi- tionally or alternatively, the radiologist may combine a 2D mammogram image, whether Mp or Ms, with a 3D projec- tion, or with selected reconstructed images, in order to obtain a customized merged image that highlights both calcifications and various tissue structures in the breast. Filters applied to each type of image can further highlight the types of structures or features in the merged image that are generally most prevalent or most readily discerned in the respective source image type. [0039] The display system 5 may be part of a standard acquisition workstation (e.g., of acquisition system 1), or of a standard (multi-display) review station that is physically remote from the acquisition system 1. In some embodi- ments, a display connected via a communication network may be used, for example, a display of a personal computer or of a so-called tablet, smart phone or other hand-held device. [0042] Thus, the system 1, which is described as for purposes of illustration and not limitation in this patent specification, is capable of receiving and displaying selec- tively tomosynthesis projection images Tp, tomosynthesis reconstruction images Tr, a synthesized mammogram image Ms, and/or mammogram (including contrast mammogram) images Mp, or any one or sub combination of these image types. The system 1 employs software to convert (i.e., reconstruct) tomosynthesis images Tp into images Tr, soft- ware for synthesizing mammogram images Ms, and soft- ware for merging a set of images to provide a merged image that displays, for every region of the merged image, the most relevant feature in that region among all images in the source image set. The objects and features of interest may include, for example, spiculated lesions, calci- fications, and the like. Various systems and methods are currently well known for computerized detection of abnor- malities in radiographic images, such as those disclosed by Giger et al. in RadioGraphics, May 1993, pp. 647-656; Giger et al. in Proceedings of SPIE, Vol. 1445 (1991), pp. 101-103; U.S. Pat. Nos. 4,907,156, 5,133,020, 5,343,390, and 5,491,627, each of which being hereby incorporated by reference in its entirety. [0043] FIG. 2 is a diagram which pictorially illustrates the merging of image data from a tomosynthesis reconstruction image data set Tr, comprising tomosynthesis slices 10A to 10N, with image data from a mammogram 20, in this case a synthesized mammogram Ms. For ease of description, filters are not shown in this example. The tomosynthesis image data set Tr and synthesized mammogram Ms are forwarded to the region compare and image merge processor 6, which evaluates each of the source images for which a merged image is to be generated (i.e., whether automatically, or based on a specific user commend) in order to (1) identify the objects and features of interest in each image for those that may be considered a 'most relevant' feature for possible inclusion in the merged image based upon the application of one or more CAD algorithms (as described above), (2) identifies respective pixel regions in the images that contain the identified features, and (3) thereafter compares the images on a region by region basis, searching for that image with the most desirable display data for each respective region. [0044] As discussed above, the image with the most desirable display data may be an image with a highest pixel value, a lowest pixel value, or which has been assigned a threshold value or weight based on the application of a CAD algorithm to the image. When the image with the most desirable display data for that region is identified, the pixels of that region are copied over to the corresponding region of the merged image. Title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR DISPLAYING AND NAVIGATING BREAST TISSUE IMAGES USING SYNTHESIZED 2D IMAGING
Technical_field
[0001] This disclosure relates generally to medical imaging systems and methods, and more particularly to systems and methods for displaying and navigating breast tissue images using synthesized 2D imaging.

Background Art
[0002] In recent years, digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) has become widely accepted for screening purposes due to its ability to reduce artifacts caused by overlapping breast tissue. DBT generates reconstructed 3D volumes, typically referred to as "tomosynthesis" reconstructions, by scanning the breast from multiple angles while taking low-dose x-ray projections. These projections can be used to reconstruct cross-sectional views of the breast tissue, reducing cluttering by overlying tissues and improving detection rates compared to conventional 2D mammography. [0003] However, despite these advantages, there remains room for improvement in how clinicians interact with tomographic data sets during clinical practice. For example, it may sometimes be difficult to visualize lesions or abnormalities within the densest parts of the breast where the signal-to-noise ratio is reduced. Similarly, certain types of tumors may not have sufficient density differences relative to surrounding tissue to be visible on standard tomo- synthesis reconstructions. Thus, there exists a need for improved techniques for visualizing and interacting with breast tissue images.
Summary of Invention
[0004] One embodiment provides a system and method for dis- playing and navigating breast tissue images. The system and method can include obtaining a synthesized 2D image of a pa- tient's breast tissue, displaying the synthesized 2D image, receiving a selection input indicating at least one region of interest in the synthesized 2D image, and displaying, in response to the selection input at least one source image for the at least selected region(s).
[0005] Another embodiment provides a workstation for display- ing and navigating breast tissue images. The worksta- tion can include a display, at least one processor, and a non-transitory memory in communication with at least one processor and having stored therein computer readable instruc- tions that, when executed by the at least one processer, cause the workstation to perform operations including ob- taining a synthesized 2D image of a patient' s breast tissue, displaying the synthesized 2Dimage, receiving a selec- tion input indicating at least one region of interest in said synthesized 2D image, and displaying, responsive to the selection input, at least one source image for the at least sel- ected region(s). [0006] Another embodiment provides a system for acquiring, processing, displaying, and/or navigating breast tissue images. The system can include an image acquisi- tion device configured to acquire a plurality of 2D and/or 2D/3D images of a patient's breast tissue, an image proces- sing device configured to generate a synthesized 2D imag- ing model of the patient's breast tissue, and a workstation configured to obtain the synthesized 2D imaging model, display the synthesized 2D imaging model, receive a selection input indicating at least one region of the synthesized 2D im- aging model, and display, in response to the selection input at least a portion of one or more images of the plurality of 2D and 2D/3D images. [0007] Other aspects and features will become apparent from the following description, the drawings, and the claims.
Brief Description of the Drawings
[0008] FIG. 1 illustrates an exemplary system according to some embodiments;
[0009] FIGS. 2A-B illustrate examples of two-dimensional (2D) images generated from three-dimensional (3D) tomo- synthesis images according to some embodiments;
[0010] FIG. 3 illustrates a block diagram of an exemplary method for creating a synthesized 2D image according to some embodi- ments;
[0011] FIG. 4 illustrates an exemplary flowchart describing a method for displaying and navigating breast tissue images according to some embodiments;
[0012] FIG. 5 illustrates an exemplary graphical user interface (GUI) for displaying and navigating breast tissue images accord- ing to some embodiments;
[0013] FIG. 6 illustrates another exemplary GUI for display- ing and navigating breast tissue images according to some embodi- ments;
FIG. 7 illustrates yet another exemplary GUI for display- ing and navigating synthesized 2D images according to some embodiments; and
[0014] FIG. 8 illustrates still another exemplary GUI for display- ing and navigating images according to some embodiments.
Detailed Description
[0015] As described herein, various embodiments provide sys- tems and methods for displaying and navigating breast tissue images. According to some embodiments, this involves generat- ing a synthesized 2D image from a set of 2D and/or 3D tomo- synthesis images. The synthesized 2D image can then be displayed along with any number of original 2D and/or 3D to- mosynthesis images. When a user selects a particular region of the synthesized 2D image, the system displays at least a portion of the original 2D and/or 3D images containing the same region. This allows users to view and compare different vantage points of the selected area without requiring them to switch between individual 2D and/or 3D images. Additionally, because the synthesized 2D image combines information from across all of the original images, it often presents a clearer picture than would be possible from viewing just one of the original images alone.
[0016] FIG. 1 shows an exemplary system 100 for display- ing and navigating breast tissue images using synthesized 2 D imaging according to some embodiments. System 100 can include an image acquisition device 102, such as a mammogram machine, ultrasound scanner, MRI, CT scanner, PET scan- ner, optical coherence tomography (OCT), photoacoustic tomog- raphy (PAT), positron emission mammography (PEM), single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), or other suitable medical imaging modality capable of capturing images of breast tissue. Image acqui- sition device 102 can be located remotely from a workstation 104, but in some embodiments they are co-located. Workstation 104 can be configured to communicate with image acquisition device 102 via wired or wireless connec- tivity, such as Ethernet, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, etc., depending on the type of connection desired. In some cases, workstation 104 can also be communicatively coupled to one or more additional devices, such as a server 106, database 108, or storage unit 110, either directly or indirectly via network 112. Network 112 can take many forms, e.g., local-area networks, wide-area networks, intranets, internets, public switched telephone networks, cellular net- works, satellite communications links, fiber optic connections, infrared connections, radio-frequency identification (RFID) communica- tions, near-field communications, or combinations thereof.
[0017] In addition to communicating with image acqui- sition device 102 and other components, workstation 104 can additionally be connected to one or more peripherals, such as a monitor 114, keyboard 116, mouse 118, stylus 120, touchpad 122, microphone 124, speaker 126, printer 128, and/or tablet 130. Monitor 114 can be used to display images captured by image acquisition device 102, as well as synthesized 2D images created by workstation 104. Key- board 116, mouse 118, stylus/touchpad 120, and microphone 124 can serve as inputs for controlling workstation 104, al- though others may be substituted or added as needed. Printer 128 can be used to print out hard copies of images, reports, or other documents related to a patient examination. Tablet 130 can be used to capture signatures, notes, or other written docu- mentation relating to the examination.
[0018] Server 106 can be used to host software applications running on workstation 104. Database 108 can store patient records, radiology orders, exam results, prescriptions, billing informa- tion, insurance details, and so forth. Storage unit 110 can be used to store raw images, processed images, intermediate pro- cessing files, final reports, and other relevant data produced dur- ing a diagnostic session. Although shown separately, in some implementations, functions performed by server 106, database 108, and storage unit 110 can instead be implemented within workstation 104 itself.
[0019] Referring now to FIGS. 2A-B, illustrated are ex- amples of two-dimensional (2D) images generated using three- dimensional (3D) tomosynthesis images according to some embodiments. FIG. 2A depicts a synthesized 2D image 200. Synthesized 2D image 200 represents a composite image formed from portions of multiple 2D and/or 3D tomosynthe- sis images taken from different depths. Each of these component images contributes to synthesized 2D image 200 by providing a specific section, or region, to be included in the composite. In the case of 3D tomosynthesis, each contributing image is typically a slice of the 3D reconstruction. In some cases, however, the contributing images might instead come from 2D acquisitions, such as those resulting from mammograms, contrast-enhanced mammogra- phy (CEM), or other modalities. It should be noted that while synthesized 2D image 200 appears like a traditional 2D image, it actually incorporates elements from multiple images taken at different depths.
[0020] Referring again to FIG. 2B, depicted are several examples of 3D tomosynthesis images that could be used to create synthesized 2D image 200. Images 210, 220, 230, 240, and 250 represent five distinct slices from a larger 3D tomosynthesis dataset, although fewer or more slices could be utilized if desired. Regions marked with numbers 212, 222, 232, 242, and 252 correspond to areas within their respec- tive images that were chosen to be part of synthesized 2D image 200. Each of these regions was identified and extracted from its parent image before being combined with the other regions to form synthesized 2D image 200. Note that the exact boundaries defining these regions are somewhat arbitrary and can vary depend- ing on factors such as the intended use of the synthesized 2D image, the characteristics of the underlying images, and the preferences of the operator.
[0021] By way of illustration, let us consider the creation of synthesized 2D image 200 from images 210, 220, 230, and 240. First, each image is analyzed to identify potential objects of interest, such as masses, calcifications, spiculations, asymmetries, architectural distortion, skin thickening, or other suspicious findings. Next, the regions of interest are isolated from each image, and then the regions are matched against each other based on similarity metrics, such as grayscale values, texture patterns, shape, size, orientation, intensity, or other criteria. Once matching regions are found, they are assembled together into synthesized 2D image 200. If necessary, post-processing steps can be applied to enhance visibility, adjust brightness, correct for artifacts, apply filters, or undertake other manipula- tions to improve the quality of synthesized 2D image 200.
[0022] Turning back to FIG. 1, workstation 104 can include one or more processors 132, memories 134, and interfaces 136. Processors 132 can execute instructions stored in mem- ories 134 to carry out various tasks assigned to workstation 104, such as performing image processing, storing and retrieving data, sending and receiving messages, and managing hardware interactions. Memories 134 can take many forms, including volatile RAM, non-volatile ROM, magnetic disks, solid-state drives, flash drives, optical discs, tape drives, RAID arrays, SAN units, NAS devices, cloud-based stor- age, distributed file systems, or other types of persistent and transitory media. Interfaces 136 enable workstation 104 to communi- cate with external devices, such as image acquisition device 102, server 106, database 108, storage unit 110, and peripherals 114-130. Interfacing protocols can involve wired or wireless connectivity, such as USB, FireWire, Thunderbolt, SATA, PCIe, HDMI, DisplayPort, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, RFID, Near Field Com- munication, Zigbee, Z-Wave, cellular networks, satellite links, infrared transmission, or proprietary communication formats.
[0023] FIG. 3 shows a block diagram illustrating an ex- ample method 300 for creating a synthesized 2D image accor- ding to some embodiments. Method 300 begins with step 302, where a plurality of 2D and/or 30 images of a patient's breast tissue are obtained. The images can originate from a variety of sources, such as a mammogram machine, ultrasound, MRI, CT scanner, PET scanner, OCT, PAT, PEM, SPECT, DXA, or other appropriate medical imaging technology. In some cases, the images may already exist in electronic form, whereas in other instances, they may require conversion from analog signals or film scans. Depending on the nature of the images, they may be acquired individually, simultaneously, or sequentially, potentially involving moving the patient or the image acquisition device.
[0024] Moving on to step 304, the obtained images undergo comparison and analysis to determine which regions of each image should be included in the synthesized 2D image. This compari- son can be done manually by an operator or automatically using algorithms. Factors considered during comparison may include pixel intensities, textures, shapes, sizes, orientations, spatial relationships, gradients, edges, curvatures, surface normals, or other quantitative properties. The goal is to select regions that share similarities, exhibit coherent structures, or present interesting fea- tures worthy of inclusion in the synthesized 2D image.
[0025] At step 306, the identified regions are isolated from their respective images. This extraction process can occur at the level of pixels, voxels, or other basic building blocks, or at higher-level abstractions such as segments, patches, or feature maps. Isolation can be achieved through thresholding, edge detection, segmentation, masking, cropping, clipping, or other means of delimiting the extent of the region.
[0026] Step 308 involves constructing the synthesized 2D image by combining the isolated regions. This assembly can be accomplished through simple concatenation, stitching, overlaying, merging, blending, or other processes designed to integrate the constituent parts seamlessly. The order in which regions are arranged matters less than ensuring continuity and smooth transitions between adjacent areas. Some approaches may involve re-sampling or interpolating to align regions with respect to a common coordinate frame. Additional steps can be taken to refine the appearance, such as adjusting brightness, applying filters, correcting artifacts, or enhancing contrast.
[0027] Optionally, step 310 involves applying one or more post-processing operations to the synthesized 2D image. Such enhancements can address issues such as noise reduction, speckle removal, artifact correction, detail preservation, edge sharpening, gradient enhancement, histogram equalization, gamma adjustment, tone mapping, color grading, or other manipulations aimed at optimizing the image for human perception or analytical purposes. Post-processing can be performed locally or globally, affecting entire regions or specific sub-regions selectively.
[0028] Finally, at step 312, the synthesized 2D image is saved and made available for future access. This step can involve writing the image to a file, uploading it to a server, transmitting it wirelessly, saving it to a cache, duplicating it onto multiple storage devices, encrypting it for security, annotating it with metadata, associating it with a patient record, linking it to a report, or other actions facilitating retrieval and utilization later on.
[0029] Now turning to FIG. 4, illustrated is an exemplary flowchart 400 describing a method for displaying and navigat- ing breast tissue images according to some embodiments. Flow- chart 400 starts at start block 402, followed by block 404, where a synthesized 2D image of a patient 's breast tissue is obtained. This synthesized 2D image is constructed using respective areas from a plurality of 2D and/or 31 images of the patient's breast tissue. Each of the respective areas is associated with at least one source image, i.e., an image from which the respective area was imported. Source images can be derived from 2D or 3D tomosynthesis images, mammograms, CEM, or other suitable medical imaging technologies.
[0030] Block 406 follows, in which the synthesized 2D image is displayed. The synthesized 2D image can be presented on a screen, printed on paper, projected onto a surface, or rendered in holographic form, depending on the desired presentation medium.
[0031] Next comes block 408, where a selection input indica- ting at least one region of interest in the synthesized image is received. This input can arise from user interaction with a pointing device, touchscreen, voice commands, eye tracking, gestures, or other mechanisms allowing operators to indicate specific areas of interest. Selection inputs can specify coordinates, shapes, or other geometric definitions for the region(s) of interest.
[0032] Following block 408 is block 410, where at least one source image for the at least indicated region is displayed. This can occur immediately after the selection input is registered, or delayed until subsequent processing completes. The source image(s) can be displayed alongside the synthesized 2D image, replacing it temporarily, or appearing as a separate window or pane. Users can navigate the source image independently, panning, zooming, rotating, or manipulating it in other ways to gain insight into the anatomy or pathology beneath the surface.
[0033] Continuing to block 412, the method optionally determines whether additional selections have been made. If no new selections are pending, control passes to end block 414. Otherwise, the loop repeats, returning to block 408 to await further input.
[0034] Returning to block 404, the synthesized 2D image can be created using various methods. For instance, it can be built up from individual slices of a 3D tomosynthesis reconstruction, with each slice serving as a source image. Alternatively, it can combine regions from 2D mammograms or other 2D images, possibly supplemented by 3D images if available. Source images can be selected based on factors such as grayscale levels, texture patterns, anatomical landmarks, lesion characteristics, or other distinguishing features.
[0035] With regard to block 406, the synthesized 2D image can be displayed on a dedicated console, laptop, tablet, smart phone, desktop computer, or other display device. Its resolution can range from relatively low-resolution thumbnails to high-definition presentations. Color schemes can emphasize subtle variations in soft tissue, highlight calcium deposits, distinguish fatty versus glandular tissue, or adopt other visualization strategies tailored to specific needs.
[0036] Regarding block 408, the selection input can be gen- erated through direct manipulation of the synthesized 2D image, such as clicking, tapping, dragging, pinching, swiping, or other gestural interactions. Voice commands, gaze-tracking, or other indirect inputs can also suffice. Coordinate-based selection methods allow specifying precise loca- tions, while free-form drawing tools permit more flexible circling around areas of interest.
[0037] Concerning block 410, the source image can be pre- sented in isolation or superimposed over the synthesized 2D image. Zooming, panning, rotation, or other interactive controls can facilitate exploration of the source image. Different layers or windows can contain the source image and synthesized 2D image concurrently, enabling side-by-side comparisons.
[0038] Turning to block 412, the decision to continue seeking additional selections depends on the user's goals and workflow requirements. If the current task requires only a cursory review, then no further action may be warranted. On the other hand, if deeper investigation is desired, the loop continues to prompt for successive selections.
[0039] Lastly, referring to block 414, once finished examining the synthesized 2D image and its constituent source images, the user may choose to save the selected regions for future reference, annotate the images with observations, transmit them to colleagues, incorporate them into a report, or engage in other activities concluding the procedure.
[0040] Referring next to FIG. 5, illustrated is an exemplary graphical user interface (GUI) 500 for displaying and navigating breast tissue images according to embodiments of the invention. GUI 500 includes a display 502 showing a synthesized 2D image 504 of a patient's breast tissue, which can be viewed in conjunction with one or more source images 506, 508, 510, 512, 514, 516, and 518. Synthet- icized 2D image 504 was constructed from respective areas of four tomosynthesis reconstruction slices 520, 522, 524, and 526, as well as mammogram 528. Each area corresponds to a region of interest (ROI) in its respective image. ROIs are highlighted in synthesized 2D image 504 by dashed outlines 530, 532, 534, and 536. Abstract: Extended reality drive scanning (e.g., using a computerized tool), is enabled. For example, a system can comprise a processor and a memory that stores executable instructions that, when executed by the processor, facilitate performance of operations. The operations can comprise scanning, via a camera, a drive rack, wherein the drive rack comprises a group of drives. The operations can further comprise, based on an indicator light of a drive of the group of drives and an identifier of the drive, determining a maintenance status of the drive. The operations can further comprise, based on the maintenance status of the drive, generating an extended reality user interface applicable to the maintenance status of the drive.

Claims: 1. A system, comprising: a processor; and a memory that stores executable instructions that, when executed by the processor, facilitate performance of operations, comprising: scanning, via a camera, a drive rack, wherein the drive rack comprises a group of drives; based on an indicator light of a drive of the group of drives and an identifier of the drive, determining a maintenance status of the drive; and based on the maintenance status of the drive, generating an extended reality user interface applicable to the maintenance status of the drive.
2. The system of claim 1, wherein the extended reality user interface comprises an overlay on a screen of a mobile device, wherein the mobile device comprises the camera, and wherein the overlay is rendered on the screen of the mobile device in real time or stored to the memory.
3. The system of claim 2, wherein the overlay comprises a color-coded overlay.
4. The system of claim 1, wherein the extended reality user interface comprises an overlay generated via extended reality glasses.
5. The system of claim 1, wherein the extended reality user interface comprises a haptic device, and wherein the haptic device generates haptic feedback at a rate based on a distance from the drive.
6. The system of claim 5, wherein the haptic device comprises a haptic glove, a haptic ring, or another means of delivering information through haptic feedback.
7. The system of claim 1, wherein the maintenance status of the drive is determined based on a comparison of a blinking pattern of the indicator light, a color of the indicator light, a shape of the indicator light, a size of the indicator light, or a placement of the indicator light for a model of drive applicable to the drive to a data table of blinking patterns, and wherein the data table comprises blinking patterns and colors per model of the group of drives.
8. The system of claim 1, wherein the operations further comprise: in response to a change in the maintenance status of the drive, modifying the extended reality user interface based on the change in the maintenance status of the drive.
9. The system of claim 1, wherein the operations further comprise: based on the identifier of the drive, determining historical maintenance information applicable to the drive, wherein the historical maintenance information is displayed via the extended reality user interface.
10. The system of claim 1, wherein the operations further comprise: based on the maintenance status of the drive, generating a recommended action to correct a malfunction of the drive, wherein the recommended action is determined based on a comparison of the maintenance status for a model of drive applicable to the drive to a maintenance data table, and wherein the maintenance data table comprises recommended actions per model of the group of drives.
11. The system of claim 1, wherein the operations further comprise: based on the maintenance status of the drive, generating a recommended action to correct a malfunction of the drive, wherein the recommended action is determined using machine learning trained based on prior actions to correct prior malfunctions of other drives, other than the drive.
12. The system of claim 1, wherein the operations further comprise: in response to a determination that, based on the identifier of the drive, the drive is not registered in a defined drive registry, adding data applicable to the drive to the defined drive registry.
13. A non-transitory machine-readable medium, comprising executable instructions that, when executed by at least one processor, facilitate performance of operations, comprising: scanning, via a camera, a server rack, wherein the server rack comprises multiple servers; based on an indicator light of a server of the multiple servers and an identifier of the server, determining a maintenance status of the server; and based on the maintenance status of the server, generating an extended reality user interface applicable to the maintenance status of the server.
14. The non-transitory machine-readable medium of claim 13, wherein the extended reality user interface comprises an overlay on a screen of a mobile device, and wherein the mobile device comprises the camera.
15. The non-transitory machine-readable medium of claim 14, wherein the overlay comprises a color-coded overlay.
16. The non-transitory machine-readable medium of claim 13, wherein the extended reality user interface comprises an overlay on extended reality glasses.
17. A method, comprising: imaging, by a system comprising at least one processor, a drive rack, wherein the drive rack comprises drives; based on an indicator light of a drive of the drives and a unique identifier of the drive, determining, by the system, a maintenance event applicable to the drive; and based on the maintenance event, generating, by the system, an extended reality user interface applicable to the maintenance event.
18. The method of claim 17, wherein the extended reality user interface comprises a haptic device, and wherein the haptic device outputs haptic feedback at a rate based on a distance from the drive.
19. The method of claim 18, wherein the haptic device comprises a haptic glove, a haptic ring, or another means of delivering information through haptic feedback.
20. The method of claim 17, wherein the maintenance event is determined based on a comparison of a blinking pattern of the indicator light, a color of the indicator light, a shape of the indicator light, a size of the indicator light, or a placement of the indicator light for a model of drive applicable to the drive to a data table of blinking patterns, and wherein the data table comprises blinking patterns and colors per model of the drives.

Embodiments herein enable a prioritized and filtered view of drive racks in a datacenter. Rather than attending equally to all indicators signaling an unhealthy state, a system herein can enable a user to filter out the excess noise and focus on the highest-priority issues. While various racks may display comparable amber lights, the system herein can identify which of these indicators are most likely to result in a data loss or data unavailable (DUDL) situation. Further, via a system herein, a user can designate what is most important to the user and customize priority levels beyond the default settings. Thus, if a user regularly ignores a particular drive due to a known and accepted issue, the user can (e.g., via the system) reduce the visual noise associated with that known and accepted issue. For example, a system herein can determine that a seemingly useable drive has experienced frequent failures, and a user may thus fully replace the drive rather than simply rebooting it again. By leveraging embodiments herein, users are enabled to easily access drive status information either by the design of the XR interface itself or through associated screen reader technology. Alternate XR technologies, such as gloves offering haptic feedback signals, may also be utilized to further reduce user reliance on their own visual capabilities. Beyond visual acuity challenges, the use of more standardized indicators surfaced in the XR interface increases accessibility, for instance, for neurodivergent individuals. By reducing the need to mentally keep track of various indicator configurations and meanings, user attention can be more focused, and users can be less prone to distraction or overwhelm. [0001] This application relates generally to systems and methods for monitoring equipment with extended reality technologies.

Background Art
[0002] Data centers are physical facilities used to house computer servers and provide computing services over the Internet. These data centers contain racks of computers called \"servers\" which store, process, transmit, receive, and manage large amounts of electronic data, including personal data, business data, website content, social media, video streaming, online gaming, cloud storage, artificial intelligence, and more. Each server contains many components, such as processors, hard disks, power supplies, cooling units, fans, batteries, etc. When any component fails, it may cause the entire server to fail and be unavailable to users. In some cases, if a component fails, it may also trigger an alert indicating the need for replacement of the failed part. However, there are often thousands of servers in a given data center, so it can be difficult to identify which specific server needs attention and what type of repair is needed. Additionally, because each server has different types of components, each requiring its own set of diagnostic procedures, it can be challenging to determine how best to diagnose and repair individual servers without extensive training and experience.

Summary of the Disclosure
[0003] Systems and methods for enabling extended reality drive scanning (e.g., using a camera) are disclosed herein. According to aspects described herein, a system can comprise a processor and a non-transitory machine-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by the processor, perform operations. The operations can comprise scanning, via an image-capturing device, a drive rack, wherein the drive rack includes a plurality of drives. The operations can further comprise, responsive to identifying an indication light of a drive of the plurality of drives and an identifier of the drive, performing operations to determine a maintenance status of the drive. The operations may further comprise, responsive to the maintenance status of the drive, generating an augmented reality display applicable to the maintenance status of the drive.
[0004] Aspects described herein relate to systems and methods for detecting problems with various pieces of equipment, such as servers, drives, printers, medical devices, industrial machinery, automobiles, aircraft, etc. By way of example, these systems and methods may utilize sensors and/or cameras to detect changes in the condition of a piece of equipment, such as changes in temperature, vibrations, sounds, lights, etc. Based on the detected conditions, the systems and methods may generate alerts and notifications, either automatically or upon request. For example, a sensor may be placed near a printer, which detects a vibration or noise associated with paper jamming. If the sensor detects this vibration/noise, it may send an alert to a remote location, whereupon a technician may remotely view a live feed of the printer to assist the technician in troubleshooting the issue. Moreover, the sensor may monitor the printer's software and firmware for updates and notify administrators accordingly.

Abstract: Visual cue augmentation for virtual windows adds visual cues into a rendered virtual window that is displayed in a real environment. Visual cue contingent rendering reinforces connections between virtual and real objects and spaces, harmonizing a virtual window scene displayed within a real environment with the real environment. In an embodiment, a virtual window is rendered that includes the visual cues. In an embodiment, using head tracking, the virtual window changes as a viewer in the real environment changes their viewing direction. In another embodiment, a true light field display is used to present the virtual window without requiring head tracking. In an environment, a motion parallax display (MPD) is used to perform user head tracking and presenting the virtual window. In general, the virtual window that is displayed responds to a viewer's head position.

  "detailed_description": "Systems and methods are disclosed related to sensory cue augmentation for virtual windows. Sensory cue augmentation may adapt the real environment using environment cues that control the local physical environment such as lighting characteristics (color, brightness, direction, etc.), temperature, humidity, air motion, and sound. Visual cue augmentation for virtual windows adds visual cues into a rendered virtual window that is displayed in a real environment. Visual cue contingent rendering reinforces connections between virtual and real objects and spaces, harmonizing a virtual window scene displayed within a real environment with the real environment. In an embodiment, a virtual window is rendered that includes the visual cues. In an embodiment, using head tracking, the virtual window changes as a viewer in the real environment changes their viewing direction. In another embodiment, a true light field display is used to present the virtual window without requiring head tracking. In an environment, a motion parallax display (MPD) is used to perform user head tracking and presenting the virtual window. In general, the virtual window that is displayed responds to a viewer's head position.
In an embodiment, for telepresence or applications lighting in the real environment simulates lighting in a different real environment (associated with a second participant who is inserted in the virtual window scene) to harmonize the real environment with the virtual window scene.
An example use case for visual cue augmentation is video conferencing, where each viewer sees their real environment displayed and the other participants are inserted into the rendered virtual window. In contrast with conventional augmented reality techniques that insert synthesized objects into displays of the real world, the rendered virtual window recreates each participant's real environment. In contrast with virtual reality techniques that display an imaginary scene, the rendered virtual window closely matches the viewer's real environment. Furthermore, the display location is fixed (e.g., mounted on a wall of a room).
FIG. 1A illustrates a real scene 100 in a real environment including a display device displaying a virtual scene rendered with visual cues, in accordance with an embodiment. Although lines defining walls, a ceiling, and a floor in the real scene 100 end rather than extend, the actual physical environment would physically surround a viewer who is present in the real scene 100. Within the real scene 100, a virtual window 105 is displayed on a two-dimensional (2D) surface of the display device, creating an illusion of a hole, portal, or window into a virtual space or virtual environment. To reinforce a perception that the virtual scene 105 is three-dimensional (3D), visual (pictorial) cues are depicted to "connect" the real and virtual environments. The visual cues increase a viewer's perception that the virtual environment is 3D and is consistent with the real environment physically occupied by the viewer.
Visual cues rendered in the virtual window 105 shown in FIG. 1A include linear perspective and a virtual ceiling-wall intersections 115 as a continuation of real ceiling-wall intersections 110, where a perceived continuation 112 is not visible, but illustrates that the virtual and real ceiling-wall intersections are perceived as continuous by a viewer. Linear perspective describes how objects appear smaller in the distance and parallel lines converge at horizons and vanishing points. People tend to perceive incomplete elements (e.g., images, sounds) as complete, synthesizing the missing elements so as to perceive the image or sound as a whole in effect closing a gap in the incomplete elements to create complete elements. Additionally, people tend to perceive objects in alignment as forming smooth, unbroken contours. For example, when two lines meet in an illustration, the preferred interpretation is of two continuous lines: A cross is interpreted as a vertical line and a horizontal line rather than as two right angles meeting at their vertices.
A virtual wall-wall intersection 117 is rendered as a continuation of real wall-wall intersection 114 and virtual floor-wall intersections 106 are rendered as continuations of real floor-wall intersections 108. General rules of the Gestalt theory may be applied to influence how objects, shapes, and rendered images are perceived. The human mind integrates individual objects into a whole, attempting to recognize a familiar pattern or order in disorder. The general rules are similarity, proximity, closure, and continuation. In the context of the following description, visual cues may include proximity (grouping common objects together to be perceived as a single unit), similarity (similar objects are perceived as a single unit), closure (complete obstructed objects and shadows), and continuation (linear perspective and consistent alignment and size between objects and structure of the real environment with the virtual scene). Visual cues should dominate other perceptual cues that the display device is in fact 2D to successfully enable the illusion. Visual cues "connect" the real and virtual environments to increase the perception that the virtual space is 3D and harmonizes with the real environment in which the virtual window 105 is viewed.
Providing sensory cues in the virtual environment and/or the real environment harmonizes the virtual environment with the real environment. Visual cues may be rendered in the virtual scene to make the virtual environment seem a "whole" that is connected to the real environment. In an embodiment, objects are inserted into the virtual scene connecting the virtual objects to objects in the real environment. For example, chair(s) may be inserted in the virtual scene that are of the same type, and aligned to a chair(s) in the real environment. Similarly, lighting may be modeled in the virtual scene that matches the lighting in the real environment. The virtual objects and/or lighting can be inserted or generated either manually or automatically in the virtual scene. In an embodiment, elements in the real environment are scanned for use in the virtual environment using computer vision or other techniques. For example, height, color, and/or texture of the real floor can be scanned and duplicated in the virtual scene.
Additionally, auditory cues and manipulations of the real environment may be generated to make the real environment harmonize with the virtual environment. Audio sources in the virtual environment such as voices of participants or sounds of nature can be spatialized with respect to the position of the user so that their perceived location matches the visual environment. Stylized environment sounds can additionally harmonize virtual and real environment. Reverberation matching size and conditions of the environment can harmonize acoustic properties. Furthermore, objects may be inserted into the real environment connecting objects rendered in the virtual scene to real objects in the real environment. For example, chair(s) may be inserted in the real environment that are of the same type, and aligned to a chair(s) in the virtual scene. Similarly, lighting may be modeled in the real environment that matches the lighting in the virtual scene. The real objects and/or lighting can be inserted or generated either manually or automatically in the real environment. In another examples, the temperature, humidity, and air motion of the real environment may be controlled to harmonize the real environment with the virtual environment.

Various functions described herein as being performed by entities may be carried out by hardware, firmware, and/or software. For instance, various functions may be carried out by a processor executing instructions stored in memory. Furthermore, persons of ordinary skill in the art will understand that any system that performs the operations of the visual cue augmentation system 150 is within the scope and spirit of embodiments of the present disclosure.
A remote participant representation is transmitted through the network(s) 130 to a local environment. The remote attribute extraction unit 135 extracts attributes related to the remote participant and the remote environment for generating sensory cues including, without limitation, visual cues, environment cues, and images or models of the remote participant 120. The environment cues are transmitted to the environment controller 165. Examples of environment cues that the environment controller 165 may control in the local physical environment include lighting characteristics (color, brightness, direction, etc.), temperature, humidity, air motion, and sound. Other remote attributes comprise visual attributes that are provided to the renderer 140. The local attribute extraction unit 180 operates similarly to the remote attribute extraction unit 135, extracting attributes related to the local participant and local environment. Local attributes comprising visual attributes are provided to the renderer 140 and to one or more remote display environments via the network(s) 130. Local attributes related to the local environment attributes are provided to one or more remote display environments via the network (s) 130. The display 160 displays a virtual scene that is rendered by the renderer 140 and includes an image or model of the remote participant 170 along with one or more visual cues associated with the real viewing environment of the local participant. In an embodiment, the remote participant 170 may be represented as an avatar. In an embodiment, the virtual scene depicts an extension of the real viewing environment, such as the virtual ceiling-wall intersections 115, virtual wall-wall intersection 117, and/or virtual floor-wall intersections 106 shown in FIG. 1A.
In an embodiment, the virtual scene is rendered to simulate the lighting of the real environment detected by the sensor(s) 175. The remote participant 120 may be inserted into the virtual scene as the remote participant 170 and be relit to match the lighting in the real environment. However, in some cases, it may be necessary to instead adapt the real environment to match the lighting of the remote participant 120. For example, if a colored light exists in the remote environment, a similar colored light may be controlled in the local environment rather than attempting to remove the colored lighting from a representation of the remote participant 120. The colored light may be simulated using an actual light or by the display 160. In an embodiment, the environment controller 165 generates a visual cue comprising modifying the lighting of the real environment to simulate lighting in the virtual scene. In an embodiment, the environment controller 165 generates a sensory cue comprising at least one of a sound, temperature, air motion, or humidity modification of the real environment to simulate a condition in the remote environment depicted by the virtual scene.
FIG. 2A illustrates a display presenting a virtual window 200 in the real environment rendered with visual cues, in accordance with an embodiment. Objects functioning or moving in the same direction appear to belong together, that is, the individual objects are perceived as a single unit (e.g., a flock of birds). For example, as shown in FIG. 2A, a real animated pattern 210 (e.g., moving banner) continues into the virtual window 200 as a visual cue 205.
FIG. 2B illustrates a display presenting a virtual window 220 in the real environment rendered with visual cues, in accordance with an embodiment. FIG. 2C illustrates a display presenting a virtual window 220 in the real environment rendered with visual cues, in accordance with an embodiment. People tend to organize objects with similar qualities into a perceptual group and interpret the individual objects as a whole. The real objects 245 (stanchions) in the real environment are perceived as a group and the group of the stanchions is continued, being rendered as a visual cue 235 in the virtual window 235, so that the real and virtual stanchions are perceived as a single object.

"Texture" is a regular variation in material and/or geometry such as the grain in wood floors or a "uniform" pattern of gravel on the ground. When the lighting in the virtual scene "matches" lighting in the real environment, the immersion and realism are improved for a viewer of the virtual scene in the real environment. Conversely, in some cases it may be desirable to modify lighting in the real environment to match lighting in the remote environment to provide an immersive experience for the viewer in the real environment.
FIG. 3A illustrates a display presenting a virtual window 300 in the real environment with a controlled light source 320, in accordance with an embodiment. To emphasize visual consistency, the real environment can be modified to "match" the illumination that the display 160 casts into the real environment. A physical window's light output can be described by a "light field," and the light field may be computed as a rendering problem with multiple views. Given an estimate of the lighting in the real environment, the "missing" light that would be present if the light field were perfect can be computed. The lower frequency, and potentially mis-colored light field, produced by the display 160 can be subtracted to produce a desired result in the real environment. Instead of directly measuring the lighting in the real environment, images of the real environment may be captured and inverted to infer the underlying lighting model via inverse rendering. The lighting model can be used to aid in developing information needed to understand how to light the real environment to derive a desired result. In an embodiment, smart lighting may be implemented in the real environment and controlled by the environment controller 165 to bring the real environment into a more consistent appearance where the light field of the display 160 is more accurate. In an embodiment, additional head tracking data corresponding to a view location of an additional participant is received from a display system in an additional real viewing environment. For example, the remote participant representation comprises the additional head tracking data associated with the remote participant 120 that is transmitted from the remote environment via the network(s) 130.
In an embodiment, a representation of the additional participant is received, the at least one lighting contribution is extracted from the representation, and lighting within the real viewing environment is controlled to simulate the at least one lighting contribution. In an embodiment, the representation is an image, such as a virtual window, and the at least one lighting contribution is extracted using inverse rendering. In an embodiment, the representation is rendered to match the real environment lighting.
At step 365, the rendered virtual scene is displayed on a display device installed at a fixed location in the real viewing environment. In an embodiment, the real viewing environment is adapted by controlling lighting using the display device. In an embodiment, the real viewing environment is adapted by controlling lighting using an additional device. In an embodiment, the display device is one of a head-tracked stereoscopic display, true light field display, or a motion parallax display.
In an embodiment, at least one of steps 355, 360, or 365 is performed on a server or in a data center and the virtual scene is streamed to a user device. In an embodiment, at least one of steps 355, 360, or 365 is performed within a cloud computing environment. In an embodiment, the virtual scene is used for training, testing, or certifying a neural network employed in a machine, robot, or autonomous vehicle. In an embodiment, at least one of steps 355, 360, or 365 is performed on a virtual machine comprising a portion of a graphics processing unit.
Sensory cue augmentation for virtual windows adds visual cues into a rendered virtual window and/or environment cues including at least one of a sound, temperature, air motion, or humidity modification of the real environment to simulate a condition in the virtual environment. Visual cue contingent rendering reinforces connections between virtual and real objects and spaces, harmonizing a virtual window scene displayed within a real environment with the real environment. In an embodiment, lighting in the real environment is controlled to harmonize with lighting in a remote real environment.
Parallel Processing Architecture
FIG. 4 illustrates a parallel processing unit (PPU) 400, in accordance with an embodiment. The PPU 400 may be used to implement the sensory cue augmentation system 150. The PPU 400 may be used to implement one or more of the display 160, sensor(s) 175, local attribute extraction unit 180, a renderer 140, environment controller 165, remote attribute extraction unit 135, network(s) 130, and sensor(s) 125 within the sensory cue augmentation system 150. In an embodiment, the PPU 400 is a multi-threaded processor that is implemented on one or more integrated circuit devices. The PPU 400 is a latency hiding architecture designed to process many threads in parallel. A thread (e.g., a thread of execution) is an instantiation of a set of instructions configured to be executed by the PPU 400. In an embodiment, the PPU 400 is a graphics processing unit (GPU) configured to implement a graphics rendering pipeline for processing three-dimensional (3D) graphics data in order to generate two-dimensional (2D) image data for display on a display device.   "detailed_description": "[0030] Aspects of the present disclosure relate to visual cue augmen- tation for virtual windows. A virtual window is a graphical element that appears as a transparent surface allowing a user to see behind it, similar to a physical window. However, unlike a physical window, a virtual window does not physically exist in the real world. Instead, it exists solely as a digital construct within a computer program or application. When viewed through a virtual window, the user sees a combination of the real-world environment behind the window and virtual content superimposed over it. This virtual content could take many forms, ranging from simple text overlays to complex three-dimensional models or even entire scenes. Virtual windows have numerous practical applications in fields such as gaming, education, entertainment, simulation, and training. They offer innovative ways to immerse users in new worlds, enhance learning experiences, and improve interactions with digital information. However, there remains a need for developing techniques that make virtual windows appear more realistic and intuitive, thus elevating the overall user experience.
[0031] To achieve greater realism and immersion in virtual windows, several key challenges must be addressed. Firstly, virtual windows often struggle to convincingly mimic the appearance of physical windows, leading to noticeable differences in texture, transparency, and reflections. Secondly, the relationship between the virtual content inside the window and the real-world environment beyond it needs improvement. Currently, virtual windows frequently fail to accurately represent how physical windows interact with their surroundings, resulting in unnatural transitions and inconsistencies. Thirdly, the lack of dynamic responses to changing lighting conditions hinders the perceived authenticity of virtual windows. Lastly, the inability to effectively incorporate contextual details about the real-world environment limits the depth and richness of the virtual window experience. Addressing these shortcomings requires innovative approaches to rendering, physics-based modeling, and contextual awareness, all of which will be discussed below.
[0032] Various solutions have been proposed to address these chal- lenges, focusing primarily on advancements in rendering tech- niques, physics engines, and AI-driven simulations. While these developments have contributed positively, significant gaps remain. Current solutions typically rely heavily on static pre-computed simu- lations and do not fully account for the complexities of real-world dynamics, leading to limited flexibility and accuracy. Moreover, most existing implementations require extensive computational resources, hindering performance in resource-constrained devices. Therefore, a continued focus on optimizing algorithms, leveraging edge computing, and integrating advanced sensors is crucial for widespread adoption. Another critical challenge lies in ensuring seamless interoperability among diverse platforms and ecosystems, necessitating standardization efforts and open communica- tion protocols. Furthermore, addressing ethical considerations related to privacy, security, and accessibility will become increasingly important as these technologies evolve.
[0033] There has therefore been a need for a solution that addresses the aforementioned problems. The following presents a comprehensive overview of the current state of virtual windows, highlighting areas of progress and ongoing challenges. Then, a novel technique for visually augmenting virtual windows is introduced, offering a range of benefits in terms of realism, interactivity, and usability. This innovation leverages cutting-edge technologies, including artificial intelligence, computer vision, and machine learning, to create highly sophisticated and responsive virtual windows. The discussion then delves deeper into the implementation details of this technique, covering the underlying principles, algorithmic components, and potential applications. The conclusion summarizes the significance of this breakthrough and outlines future directions for research and development.
[0034] Aspects of the present disclosure provide a robust and efficient framework for generating high-quality virtual windows that seamlessly integrate with the real world. This framework utilizes a unique combination of machine learning algorithms and com- puter vision techniques to produce photorealistic results, enabling a wide range of applications. The system begins by capturing reference images of the target environment, which are then processed using deep learning networks to generate accurate representations of the desired virtual window style. The generated model is subsequently applied to other locations, producing consistent and coherent results. Key features of this approach include its ability to handle varying lighting condi- tions, support for multiple styles and resolutions, and effec- tive handling of occlusions. The framework offers a flexible and scalable solution for creating high-quality virtual windows, making it well-suited for use in various scenarios, from architectural visualizations to video game development. The code accompanying this description provides a clear understanding of the implementation details and enables easy replication of the results.
[0035] The present disclosure describes a system and method for generating a virtual window. A virtual window is a graphical element that presents a virtual scene that is visible through the virtual window. The virtual window is placed in a real environment so that the virtual scene is partially obscured by the real environment. The virtual window may be designed to look like a physical window, such as a rectangular shape with edges, corners, frames, and possibly glass-like material properties. Alternatively, the virtual window may have a different shape, size, color, texture, or transparency level depending on the intended purpose of the virtual window. For instance, a virtual window might resemble a picture frame, a mirror, a screen, or any other type of translucent object. Regardless of its form, the primary function of a virtual window is to reveal a virtual scene that coexists with the real environment. Thus, a virtual window is distinct from a traditional screen, which only displays a single two-dimensional image and lacks spatial relationships with the surrounding environment.
[0036] In addition to serving as a portal to a virtual scene, a virtual window may also convey information, tell stories, or showcase products. It may contain animations, videos, games, advertisements, educational materials, or any other kind of digital content. Depending on the context, a virtual window may be stationary or movable, appearing as if it were attached to a wall, floating freely, or mounted on a mobile device. Some virtual windows may change their contents dynamically based on factors like time, location, or user actions. Others may respond to external stimuli, such as sound waves, temperature fluctuations, or movement detection. Virtual windows can be found indoors or outdoors, and they can vary greatly in scale, from small windows on smartphones to massive installations in public spaces. The diversity of virtual windows reflects their versatility and adaptability to suit a wide array of creative visions and functional requirements.
[0037] The concept of virtual windows intersects with various disciplines, including art, architecture, engineering, psychology, and computer science. Artists employ virtual windows as a tool for exploring new modes of expression and storytelling. Architects utilize them to reimagine urban landscapes and interior designs. Engineers leverage them for visualization, simulation, and prototyping. Psychologists study human perception and behavior in relation to virtual windows. Computer scientists develop algorithms and frameworks for generating and interacting with virtual windows. Each discipline brings unique perspectives and contributions to the evolution of virtual windows, driving innovations that blur the boundaries between the physical and digital realms.
[0038] Referring now to FIG. 1A, a virtual window 102 is shown according to aspects of the present disclosure. The virtual window 102 is depicted as being located in a real environment 104. In this particular example, the virtual window 102 is positioned on a desk 106 in a conference room 108. The virtual window 102 is made up of pixels 110 arranged in a grid pattern. The virtual window 102 displays a virtual scene 112 that includes a number of objects 114, such as furniture, walls, and other items. The virtual scene 112 is a collection of three-dimensional objects that occupy space and interact with each other. The virtual window 102 is semi-transparent, meaning that the real environment 104, specifically the desk 106, is visible beneath the virtual window 102. This semi-transparency creates the illusion that the virtual window 102 is a thin layer of glass or plastic separating the virtual scene 112 from the real environment 104.
[0039] In order to maintain consistency with the real environment 104, the virtual window 102 incorporates visual cues 116. The visual cues 116 are characteristics that connect the virtual window 102 to its surroundings. They help establish a sense of continuity and coherence between the virtual scene 112 and the real environment 104. Examples of visual cues 116 include similarities, proximity, closure, and continu- ation. Similarity refers to shared attributes between the virtual window 102 and the real environment 104. Proximity indicates how close the virtual window 102 is to adjacent surfaces or ob- jects in the real environment 104. Closure implies that the virtual window 102 completes or closes off a gap or opening in the real environment 104. Continuation suggests that the virtual window 102 extends or continues a line, curve, or pattern found in the real environment 104. By incorporating these visual cues 116, the virtual window 102 becomes less distinguishable from the real environment 104, fostering a more cohesive and immersive experi- ence.

This feature enhances the overall visual fidelity of the virtual window 102, making it easier for observers to navigate and understand the virtual scene 112.

Another method employs holographic projection, where light is manipulated to create a three-dimen- sional image suspended in mid-air. Projection mapping is anoth- er technique that wraps digital content around physical objec- tives, blending the lines between the real and virtual worlds. Light Field Displays (LFDs) project individual rays of light onto the viewer's eyes, recreating a complete image without glasses or headsets. Motion Parallax Displays (MPDs) track the viewer's head movements, adjusting the projected image to create a convincing sense of depth. Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) place a miniature projector or lenses near the wearer's eyes, delivering an immersive experience via direct-to-eye projection. These techniques offer distinct advantages and trade-offs regarding cost, complexity, resolution, portability, and field-of-view.
[0042] The virtual window 102 can be populated with a variety of content. Textures, patterns, shapes, colors, and transpar- ency levels can be customized to fit specific themes, contexts, or brand identities. Real-time data feeds can update the content in synchronization with events, weather forecasts, stock market trends, or social media streams. Video playback can show movies, live broadcasts, or recorded footage. Three-dimensional models can depict product designs, architectural plans, or historical reconstructions. Interactive elements can respond to touch gestures, voice commands, or biometric inputs. Animation sequences can create engaging narratives, visual effects, or tutorials. Audio tracks can play music, narrations, or ambient sounds. Incorporating relevant content makes the virtual window 102 a valuable tool for advertising, education, entertainment, and communication.
[0043] In some cases, the virtual window 102 may be subject to environmental influences. Lighting conditions, such as day-night cycles, sun angles, or indoor illumination, affect the brightness, shadows, and color palette of the virtual window 102. Weather phenomena, like rain, snow, or fog, can alter the visibility, refraction, and distortion of the virtual window 102. Temperature variations, humidity, or air currents can impact the transparency, clarity, or stability of the virtual window 102. Physical contact, such as touching or tapping, can modify the appearance, responsiveness, or feedback of the virtual window 102. Environmental factors introduce variability and dynamism to the virtual window 102, making it more relatable and engaging."

Abstract: Aspects of the present disclosure relate to instant boundary creation for a virtual reality (VR) experience. An artificial reality (XR) system, while rendering an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) environment, can scan and gather visual characteristic data for a user's real-world environment in the background. When the XR system detects an intent to enter VR mode (e.g., by launching a VR application), the XR system can generate a recommendation for a boundary for the real-world space, which can include a type of interaction mode (e.g., moveable or stationary mode). Based on the user's response to the recommendation, the XR system can prompt the user to scan the real-world space further and/or manually adjust the boundary, while continuing to scan and gather visual characteristic data in the background. Some implementations can alternatively or additionally automatically relocalize a real-world space based on a generated boundary.

Claims: 1. A method for automatically generating a boundary for a virtual reality experience, the method comprising:
rendering, on an artificial reality system of a user, an artificial reality environment, the artificial reality envi- ronment including one or more virtual objects overlaid on a view of a real-world space;
while rendering the artificial reality environment, auto- matically detecting characteristics of the real-world space by scanning the real-world space as the artificial reality system is moved;
detecting a trigger indicative of an intent to execute the virtual reality experience on the artificial reality sys- tem;
