Title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR OBJECT DETECTION BY MACHINE LEARNING ALGORITHM
Technical Field
The present disclosure relates to systems and methods for object detection by means of a machine learning algorithm.
Background Art
In vehicles equipped with sensors such as cameras, radar sensors or lidar sensors, there is a need to detect objects within the field of view of these sensors. This can be done by means of classical image processing algorithms, which may not always provide sufficient performance due to their limited ability to learn complex patterns. Machine learning algorithms, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs), are increasingly used for this purpose. These CNNs are capable of detecting various types of objects in images captured by the sensors. However, they require large amounts of labeled training data, which is often expensive to obtain, particularly if the goal is to recognize specific classes of objects such as pedestrians, bicycles, cars, etc. Furthermore, it takes considerable computing power and memory resources to implement these models in real-time applications.
Summary of Invention
A computer-implemented method for providing a machine-learning-algorithm for object detection is disclosed. The method includes training a first machine-learning algorithm for object detection by using a first training data set of single images based on sensor data of a vehicle environment. Additionally, a second machine-learning algorithm for object detection is trained by using a second data set including multiple time-series images. An input side section and an output side section of the second machine-learning algorithm comprise a predetermined number of layers derived from the trained-first machine-learning algorithm. The input side section of the second machine-learning algorithm has frozen weight values. Moreover, the second machine-learning algorithm further comprises a predetermined number of additional layers inserted between the aforementioned input side section and the output side section.
Another aspect of the present invention provides a computer implemented method for object detection by a machine-learning algorithm. The method includes providing a first data set consisting of multiple time-series images based on sensor data of a vehicle environment and applying a machine-learning algorithm trained according to the above described method to the first data set consisting of multiple time-series images for object detection. Finally, a second data set representing a result of the detected objects or annotated objects in the multiple time-series images is outputted.
Yet another aspect of the present invention provides a system for providing a machine-learning algorithm for an object detection. The system includes a training computer configured to train a first machine-learn-ing algorithm for object detection by using a first training-data set of single images based on sensor data of an automobile environment. Further-more, the training computer is configured to train a second-machine-learning algorithm for object detection by using a second-training data set including multiple time-series images. An-input side section and an output side section of the-second machine-learning algorithm comprise a predeter-mined number of layers derived from the trained first-machine-learning algorithm. The input side section of the-second machine-learning algorithm has frozen weight values. Moreover-the second machine-learning algorithm further comprises a-predetermined number of additional layers inserted betweenthe aforementioned input side section and the outputside-section.
Yet another aspect of the present invention provides-a system for object detection by a machine-learning-algorithm. The system includes a data receiving device-configured to receive a first data set consisting of multiple time-series-images based on sensor data of an automobile envi-ronment. A computer is configured to apply a machine-learning algorithm, trained in accordance with the afore-described method, to the first data set consisting of multiple time-seriessimages for object detection. An output unit is con-fgured to output a second data set representing a result-of the detected objects or annotated objects in themultiple time-series images.
Still yet another aspect of the present invention pro-vides a computer program with program code in order tocarry out the method for object detection by a machinelearning algorithm according to any preceding claim whenthe computer program is run on a computer.
Accordingly, the present invention aims to improve object detection by machine learning algorithms while reducing computational complexity and memory requirements. It achieves this through the use of pre-trained deep learning models that can be fine-tuned for specific tasks without requiring extensive retraining. By utilizing existing knowledge from related domains, the approach reduces the amount of required training data, making it more efficient and cost-effective. The proposed method involves transferring learned features from a source domain (e.g., single-image-based object detection) to a target domain (e.g., multi-frame video sequences). This transfer enables the model to leverage the strengths of both domains and adapt to new scenarios where only few annotated samples are available. The method uses a combination of feature extraction and adaptation techniques to align the representations across different modalities. Feature extraction is performed using a pre-trained backbone network, and then an adaptation module refines the extracted features for the target task. To ensure robustness against variations in appearance and motion, temporal information is incorporated into the adaptation process. This results in improved performance and efficiency compared to traditional approaches that rely solely on frame-by-frame analysis. The method's architecture allows for flexible design choices regarding the choice of backbone network, adaptation module, and fusion strategy. Experimental evaluation demonstrates its effectiveness on several benchmarks, showcasing superior results under varying conditions.
Advantageous Embodiments
An advantageous embodiment of the invention proposes a method for providing a machine-learning algorithm for object recognition. According to this embodiment, a first machine-learning algorithm is trained for object recognition using a first training data set of individual images acquired from a vehicle environment. Subsequently, a second machine-learning algorithm is trained for object recognition using an additional training data set containing a plurality of sequential images. The input part and the output part of the second machine-learning algorithm contain a predefined number of layers derived from the already trained first machine-learning algorithm. The input part of the second machine-learning algorithm contains fixed weighting factors. Additionally, the second machine-learning algorithm has a predefined number of additional layers interposed between the input part and the output part.
This concept makes it possible to utilize a pre-trained machine-learning algorithm for object recognition, which has been trained on a relatively small dataset of single images, to achieve good accuracy in recognizing objects even in situations where no corresponding annotations are available during training. Since the second machine-learning algorithm does not require any additional training data other than the additional training data set of sequential images, it is significantly faster and less computationally intensive than conventional machine-learning algorithms that must be completely trained on larger datasets.
According to an advantageous variant, the training of the first machine-learning algorithm includes providing a third training data set representing the result of the object recognition with annotated objects in the individual images, and training the first machine-learning algorithm by a gradient descent optimizer that determines an extremum of a loss function for object recognition.
By adjusting the parameters of the first machine-learning algorithm so that the difference between the predicted objects and the actual objects is minimized, the first machine-learning algorithm learns how to correctly identify objects in individual images.
According to another advantageous variant, the training of the second machine-learning algorithm includes providing a fourth training data set representing the result of the object detection with annotated objects in the plurality of sequential images, and training the second machine-learning algorithm by a stochastic gradient descent optimizer that determines an extremum of the loss function for object recognition.
Through iterative adjustments of the parameters of the second machine-learning algorithm, the latter learns how to accurately identify objects in the sequential images.
According to another advantageous variant, the second machine-learning algorithm receives the plurality of sequential images of the second training data set in parallel. For example, the second machine-learning algorithm processes all images of a given sequence simultaneously rather than sequentially.
According to still another advantageous variant, the plurality of sequential images of the second training set passed through the input part of the second machine-learning algorithm are processed in parallel.
For instance, the second machine-learning algorithm propagates each image of the sequence through the input part simultaneously.
According to another advantageous variant, the plurality of sequential images processed in parallel by the input part of the second machine-learning algorithm is supplied in parallel to a first layer among the additional layers inserted between the input part and the output part of the second-machine-learning algorithm.
As a result, the second machine-learning algorithm can efficiently handle multiple frames of a sequence in parallel, thereby increasing overall throughput.
According to another advantageous variant, the first and/or second of the additional layers inserted between the input part and output part of the second machine-learning algorithm combine the plurality of sequential images processed in parallel and transmit the combined images to the output part of the second machine-learning algorithm.
Thus, the second machine-learning algorithm can synthesize the information contained in the multiple frames of a sequence before passing it to the output part, allowing for better contextual understanding and decision-making.
According to another advantageous variant, a weighted sum is formed of the output data from the output part of the first machine-learning algorithm and the output date from the output part of the second machine-learning algorithm. As a result, the prediction generated by the first machine-learning algorithm, which was trained on single images, is blended with the prediction produced by the second machine-learning algorithm, which was specifically designed to work with sequential images. This blending helps to refine the final outcome and make it more accurate.
According to another advantageous variant, the output data of the output part of the second machine-learning algorithm are weighted heavier than the output data of the output part of the first machine-learning algorithm. Consequently, the contribution of the second machine-learning algorithm, which specializes in handling sequential images, is amplified relative to the contribution of the first machine-learning algorithm, which operates primarily on single images. This ensures that the final prediction is influenced more strongly by the expert knowledge gained from working with sequential images.
According to another advantageous variant, both the first machine-learning algorithm and the second machine-learning algorithm are composed of a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN).
Both machine-learning algorithms are built upon RNN architectures, which are well-suited for processing sequential inputs like videos. They can effectively capture temporal dependencies and relationships between consecutive frames, enabling sophisticated modeling of dynamic scenes.
According to another advantageous variant, the plurality sequential images of the second training data set consists of a sequence of four to five individual images spanning a time interval of one to two seconds.
These settings allow the second machine-learning algorithm to focus on short-term interactions and dynamics within the scene, capturing important events and changes that occur rapidly. By limiting the sequence length and duration, the model becomes more agile and responsive to immediate surroundings, making it suitable for applications demanding quick reaction times.
Further advantages, features and details of the invention will become apparent from the following description and drawings.
Brief Description of Drawings
FIG. 1 shows a flowchart illustrating a computer-implemented method for providing a machine-learning al-gorithm for object detection;
FIG. 2 shows a block diagram of a system for providing a machine-learning algorithm for ob-ject detection;
FIG. 3 shows a block diagram of a system for object detection by a machine-learning algo-rithm;
FIG. 4 illustrates a flow chart of a computer-implemented method for object detection by a ma-chine-learning algorithm; and
FIGS. 5a-d show examples of a sequence of four images over a period of approximately one sec-ond.
Detailed Description of Preferred Embodiments
FIG. 1 depicts a flowchart showing a computer-implemented method 100 for providing a machine-learning algorithm for object detection. Initially, in step S102, a first machine-learning algorithm is trained for objec-recognition using a first training data set of individual images obtained from an automotive environment. Thereafter, in step S104, a second machine-learning algorithm is trained for the same purpose but using a second training data set comprising a plurality of sequential images. Specifically, the input part and the output part of the sec-ond machine-learning algorithm consist of a predefined num-ber of layers derived from the previously trained first machine-learning algorithm. The input part itself possesses frozen weighting coefficients. Furthermore, the second machine-learning algorithm incorporates a predefined number of addi-tional layers placed between the aforementioned input part and the output part. By doing so, the second machine-learning algorithm is able to tap into the expertise of the first machine-learning algorithm, which has been trained on a smaller dataset of individual images, and apply it to the context of sequential images.
FIG. 2 illustrates a block diagram of a system 200 for providing a machine-learning algorithm for object recog-nition. System 200 comprises a training computer 210 that trains a first machine-learning algorithm 212 for object recognition using a first training data set 214 of individual images obtained from an automotive environment. Simultaneously, the training computer 210 trains a second machine-learning algorithm 216 for the same purpose but using a second training set 218 com-prising a plurality of sequential images. Here again, the input part 220 and the output part 222 of the second machine-learning algorithm 216 consist of a predefined number of layers derived from the previously trained first machine-leaming algorithm 212. The input part 220 itself pos-sesses frozen weighting coefficients 224. Furthermore, the second machine-learning algorithm 216 incorporates a predefined number of additional layers 226 positioned between the aforementioned input part 220 and the output part 22. Thus, the second machine-learning algorithm 216 can draw upon the know-how of the first machine-learning algorithm 212, which has been trained on a smaller dataset 214 of individual images, and apply it to the realm of sequential images.
FIG. 3 represents a block diagram of a system 300 for object detection by a machine-learning algorithm. System 300 includes a data acquisition component 310 that acquires a first data set 312 comprising a plurality of sequential images based on sensor data of an automotive environment. Next, a computer 320 applies a machine-learning algorithm 322, trained in accordance with the aforemen-tioned method, to the first data set 312 comprising the plurality of sequential images for object detection. Ultimately, an output unit 330 transmits a second data set 332 represen-ting the result of the recognized objects or annotated objects in the plurality of sequential images.
FIG. 4 shows a flowchart depicting a computer-implemented method 400 for object detection by a machine-learning algorithm. First, in step S402, a first data set 404 is made available, which includes a plurality of sequential images based on sensor data from an automotive environment. Then, in step S406, the first data set 404 is applied to a machine-learning algorithm 408, which has been trained according to the aforementioned method, for object detection. In conclusion, in step S410, a second data set 412 representing the result of the recognized objects or annotated objects is transmitted in the plurality of sequential images.
FIGS. 5a-d illustrate examples of a sequence of four images over a span of about one second. FIG. 5a presents the first frame of the sequence, taken at t=0 s. At t=0.25 s, we see the second frame in FIG. 5b, followed by the third frame in FIG. 5c at t=0.5 s, and finally the fourth frame in FIG. 5d at t=0.75 s. Each frame captures a distinct moment in time, offering insights into the evolving scenario. Together, these images form a cohesive narrative, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the situation unfolding around the camera. By analyzing these sequential frames, observers can infer actions, movements, and changes occurring over time, gaining valuable context essential for informed decisions or interpretations. Such visual narratives are crucial in fields like surveillance, sports analytics, and event monitoring, where tracking progressions and identifying key moments is vital for effective analysis and response.
Although the preferred embodiments have been de-scribed herein with reference to the accompanying drawings, it is to be understood that the invention is not limited thereto. That is, those skilled in the art understand that varia-tions and modifications may be made to the described embodi-ments without departing from the scope and spirit of the invention. Accordingly, the foregoing descriptions should be considered exemplary only. All structural and functional equivalents of the elements discussed above should be construed as within the scope of the invention. Furthermore, well-known elements, materials, and operational procedures are not shown or described in detail to avoid obscuring aspects of the present invention. Therefore, the appended claims are intended to cover all such variations and modifica-tions that fall within the true spirit and scope of the invention.
